title: Building Your Ops Team: Cleaner, Co-Host, or Property Manager

slides.title: Staff the jobs, not the titles, and test every fee against cash flow
slides.subtitle: Lesson OP.7. Building Your Ops Team: Cleaner, Co-Host, or Property Manager
meta: Cedar Ridge, the course's example house (hypothetical)
Education only. Not legal, licensing, tax, or insurance advice.
slides.notes:
After this lesson you can list every job a stay requires. You'll name who does each one, and you'll name a backup.

You'll also decide what access each person gets. That covers the platform, money, guest data, and keys. Then you'll compare a set of hired vendors against a co-host or a manager, using your own numbers. And you'll find the places where you'd pay two people for the same task.

Cedar Ridge, the course's example house, makes this concrete. Its owners, Maya and Chris, live about two hours from the house, and both work full time. So the question of who does the work is real for them. We'll run their numbers four or five ways and watch what a percentage fee does to cash flow on the DSCR loan.

The retained lessons 6.1 Cleaners and 6.2 Handyman cover how to find and train those vendors. This lesson is about fitting the whole team together for a house you own.

slides.title: List the jobs every stay needs before you choose a job title
items: Every stay: turnover cleaning, laundry, restocking, a condition check, guest messaging
On demand: repairs, lockouts, supply runs, access for vendors
Around the clock: emergencies and anything that can't wait until morning
On a schedule: inspections, bookkeeping, tax filings, permit renewals
Owner-only: pricing approval, compliance, bank and platform ownership, team review

box.label: The owner keeps responsibility
box.text: You can delegate work. The owner still holds the house, the loan, and the platform account, and answers to the city, the lender, and the insurer.

slides.notes:
"Should I hire a co-host or a property manager?" is the wrong first question. Those titles cover very different scopes, and the scopes overlap. One co-host does messaging only. Another does everything but cleaning. You can't compare them until you know the jobs.

So start with the list of jobs every stay needs. A turnover is the clean and reset between one guest and the next. I group them by when they happen. Some happen every stay. Some happen on demand. Some happen at any hour. Some run on a schedule, like the filters, the alarms, the grill, the deck, and the water heater.

Then look at the last group. Pricing approval, compliance decisions, the bank and platform accounts, and reviewing how the team performs stay with the owner.

You can hand off a lot of work. You can't hand off responsibility for it. The owner keeps title to the house, the loan, and the platform account. When the city, the lender, or the insurer has a question, they ask the owner.

slides.title: Map each job to a role, then give every guest-facing role a trained backup
slides.keyline: Backups get access before the emergency. Cedar Ridge's backups are on slide 14.
rows: Per turnover, often at a premium
After-hours first response within a set drive time
Retainer, or part of a co-host scope
Owner time, co-host fee, or a service
Par levels (minimum stock) of consumables and linens
slides.notes:
Once you have the job list, write one name beside each job. Then write a second name.

That's the backup rule. Every role that touches a guest stay needs a backup who has already been trained and given access. The access part matters. Say your cleaner gets sick at 7 a.m. You don't want to be adding the backup to the calendar and texting a door code while a guest drives in.

This table shows the usual roles for a small owned short-term rental. Look at the payment column. Some roles are per turnover, some are a retainer, some are a percentage or owner time. That mix is where costs hide later, so write it down now.

Notice that one person can hold several roles. At Cedar Ridge, the handyman is also the emergency contact and does the inspections. That's fine. What matters is that every role has a name and a backup. You'll see Cedar Ridge's backups on slide 14.

slides.title: Decide five kinds of access separately, and give each person the least they need
items: Platform access: see the calendar, message guests, or change prices and the listing
Spending authority: how much, on what, without asking
Guest data: names, phone numbers, messages, and whether they store any of it
Keys and codes: keys, lock codes, the owner's closet code, the Wi-Fi admin login
After-hours responsibility: who answers at 2 a.m., and how fast they must get there

box.label: The common mistake
box.text: Full platform access for someone who only needed a calendar. Access given for convenience is hard to take back later.

slides.notes:
Every person on the team needs some access. The rule is to give each one the least access that still lets them do the job.

There are five kinds of access, and they aren't the same thing. Someone can have a lock code and no platform access. Someone can message guests and have no spending authority. Decide each one separately.

A common mistake is giving full platform access to someone who only needed the calendar. It feels easier at the start. Then it's hard to take back without friction, because it looks like you've stopped trusting them.

Guest names, phone numbers, and messages should stay in the platform or the PMS, your property management software. Sam's OP.4 lesson on tech stack architecture shows where messages and tasks live. From that lesson, note where each team member logs in. Then you can set access there instead of sharing passwords.

And after-hours responsibility is a real assignment. Somebody's phone is on at 2 a.m., and you need to know whose.

slides.title: Airbnb's co-host levels let a cleaner see the calendar without touching money
columns: What it allows, per Airbnb's help pages
rows: Manage listing and calendar, message guests, view payouts, manage other co-hosts, submit reimbursement requests
A vetted, contracted full-service co-host or manager
View (not edit) the calendar and message guests
A messaging co-host or a cleaner-coordinator
View the calendar and check-in and checkout details; not shown as a co-host on the listing
A cleaner or handyman who needs the turnover schedule

box.label: Check before you rely on it
box.text: Summarized from Airbnb's help pages, 2026-09-25. Confirm labels in your own account.

slides.notes:
Airbnb lets a listing owner add co-hosts at different permission levels. Its co-host page describes three.

Full access lets someone manage the listing and the calendar, message guests, and view payouts and transaction history. They can also manage other co-hosts and their permissions, and submit reimbursement requests for you. That's a lot. It fits a full-service co-host or manager you've vetted and signed an agreement with.

Calendar and messaging access lets someone view the calendar, without editing it, and message guests. That fits a messaging co-host.

Calendar access lets someone see the calendar and the check-in and checkout details. These co-hosts don't show on the listing. That fits a cleaner or a handyman who only needs the turnover schedule.

One caution. These descriptions summarize Airbnb's help pages as of September 25, 2026. Airbnb changes these screens, so check the labels in your own account before you rely on them.

For Cedar Ridge, the cleaner gets calendar access. If Maya and Chris ever add a messaging co-host, that person gets calendar and messaging access. Nobody gets full access unless they're managing the listing under a written agreement.

slides.title: The owner answers for every co-host, and Airbnb can pay co-hosts before you
items: The listing owner is responsible for co-hosts, including ones a full-access co-host adds
Only the listing owner can set up co-host payouts, at any permission level
When host earnings exceed co-host payouts, co-hosts are paid first
Co-hosts can't view or change the owner's payout method or taxpayer information
The host stays responsible for a co-host's actions from before the co-host was removed

box.label: Monthly habit
box.text: A wrong payout percentage goes straight out the door. Check the co-host payout math every month.

slides.notes:
A few more points from Airbnb's help pages matter for owners.

First, you're responsible for your co-hosts. That includes co-hosts that a full-access co-host added on their own. Airbnb's co-host page tells owners to choose them with care.

Second, only the listing owner can set up co-host payouts. You can set them up for a co-host at any permission level.

Third, payment order. When your earnings on a booking are bigger than the co-host payout, the co-host gets paid first. That's convenient for them. It also means a wrong percentage gets paid out before your share, on every booking. So check the payout math monthly.

Fourth, co-hosts can't see or change your payout method or your taxpayer information. That stays with you.

And the Co-Host Additional Terms say you stay responsible for what a co-host did before you removed them.

slides.title: A short written agreement answers the questions you'd otherwise argue about later
rows: Which jobs from the OP.7.1 list, by name; anything else is extra
Per turnover, hourly, flat, or percentage; if a percentage, of what
The OP.8 checklist, with photo proof of each room
Reply time and on-site time, by hour of day
A dollar limit per item and per month, and the emergency exception
General liability; workers' comp and auto may apply by state
Guest data stays in the platform or property software; deleted on termination
Individual lock codes, changed when someone leaves
Who covers when they're sick or booked, and who pays the difference
Notice, keys returned, platform removal, bookings and records handed over
slides.notes:
A handshake works until the first damaged sofa. So every role that touches the house or guests gets a short written agreement. It doesn't need to be long. It needs to answer the questions you'd otherwise argue about.

Scope comes first. List the jobs by name from the job list. Anything not listed is extra or not included.

The fee base catches people. A percentage of what? Nightly revenue only? Nightly revenue plus cleaning fees? Payout after platform fees? Those give different numbers, and I'll show you how different in the Cedar Ridge math.

The quality standard is the OP.8 checklist, with photos. Insurance means general liability for anyone working in the house. Workers' compensation and auto coverage may apply, depending on the state and how the vendor is set up.

Data handling means guest details stay in the platform or your property management software. Keys and codes are individual. No shared master code. When someone leaves, their code gets changed.

And termination covers the handover: keys, platform removal, future bookings, and records.

slides.title: Vet before you sign, and ask whether a paid co-host needs a license in your state

left.head: Vetting, before the agreement
items: Two references from other STR owners, not friends
Proof of insurance
One paid trial turnover to the OP.8 standard before the first guest
Ask a co-host how many properties they handle, and who covers two emergencies at once

right.head: Licensing and coverage
items: Some states and cities require a real estate or property management license to manage a rental for someone else for pay
That can apply to a co-host or manager
Confirm with an attorney or the state licensing board before you sign
Ask the insurer what vendor coverage your policy requires

slides.notes:
Vetting runs before the agreement, not after.

Ask for two references from other short-term rental owners. Friends don't count. Ask for proof of insurance and look at it. Ask the cleaner to do one paid trial turnover to the OP.8 standard before the first guest ever arrives.

For a co-host, ask how many properties they handle. Then ask who covers when two emergencies happen at the same time. The answer tells you whether there's a real backup or just one busy person.

Then the licensing question. Some states and cities require a real estate or property management license for anyone who manages a rental for someone else for pay. That can apply to a co-host or a manager. I can't tell you the rule for your state. An attorney or the state licensing board can, so ask before you sign.

slides.title: Vendor set, co-host, or manager: know what each covers so you don't pay twice
rows: Owner hires each role and does messaging and approvals
Some or all of messaging, coordination, restocking, local response; cleaning often billed separately
Scope varies widely, so the agreement matters
Listing, pricing, messaging, coordination, owner statements; often own vendors

box.label: How paying twice happens
box.text: A handyman retainer kept after the co-host's scope includes inspections. A messaging service while the co-host also answers guests. A manager's supply markup while the cleaner bills for supplies. Fix: a task ledger with exactly one payer per job.

slides.notes:
There are three broad setups for an owned house.

A vendor set means you hire each role yourself and coordinate them. You do the guest messaging and the approvals. It costs the least in fees and the most in your time.

A co-host usually takes on some or all of messaging, coordination, restocking, and local response. Cleaning and repairs are often still billed separately. Scope varies a lot, which is why the agreement matters.

A full manager usually takes the listing, pricing, messaging, coordination, and owner statements. Many use their own cleaners and vendors, and some add markups.

Paying twice happens quietly. You add a co-host whose scope includes monthly inspections, and you keep paying the handyman's inspection retainer. That's the example we'll price at Cedar Ridge. Or a manager charges a supply markup while the cleaner also bills for supplies.

The fix is a task ledger. Write every job in one column. Beside each job, name exactly one payer. If two names show up, cut one or rewrite a scope.

slides.title: An 18% co-host swings Cedar Ridge from $5,572 to -$7,798 a year
slides.side:
Option A, vendor set: $29,209 - $23,637 = **$5,572**. Cleaner at $150 per turnover ($9,150), handyman retainer at $150 a month ($1,800). Maya messages; Chris approves and keeps the books.

The house doesn't carry an 18% co-host at the base case. Figures are before the $400/yr permit renewal.
slides.notes:
Here are the Cedar Ridge numbers. Cedar Ridge is the course's example house. The base case is the expected year: 61 stays, 212 booked nights at $300, a 3.5-night average stay. Gross booking revenue, nightly plus cleaning fees, is $74,275.

NOI is net operating income. It's revenue minus every operating cost, including the cleaner and the retainer, before the loan. Maya and Chris have two loan quotes. We test on the DSCR quote because it costs more: $23,637 a year in principal and interest.

Option A is the vendor set. A local cleaner at $150 per turnover, $9,150 a year. An on-call handyman retainer at $150 a month, $1,800 a year. Maya handles messaging. Chris handles approvals and bookkeeping. NOI is $29,209, and cash flow is $5,572. That's on the original underwriting, before the $400-a-year permit renewal.

Option B adds a full-service co-host at 18% of gross. That's $13,370. NOI drops to $15,839. After the loan, cash flow is negative $7,798. This fee, on this house and this loan, doesn't fit.

slides.title: At Cedar Ridge, any percentage fee above 7.5% of gross turns the base case negative
slides.side:
On the conventional quote ($22,763 a year), the break-even fee is **8.7%**.

If a quote is a percentage of nightly revenue only: $5,572 ÷ $63,600 = **8.8%**.
slides.notes:
This is the number I'd work out before talking to any co-host. How big a percentage fee can the base case carry before cash flow hits zero?

Start with the room you have. NOI with a vendor set is $29,209. Take out loan payments of $23,637, and there's $5,572 left. Divide that by gross booking revenue of $74,275. You get 7.5%.

So for Cedar Ridge, any percentage co-host above 7.5% of gross turns the base case negative on the DSCR loan. On the conventional quote the break-even is 8.7%. Your number will be different.

Watch the fee base. If a quote is a percentage of nightly revenue only, divide by nightly revenue instead. At Cedar Ridge that's 8.8%.

That's your ceiling. When someone quotes you 15% or 20%, you already know the base-case answer. You'd be paying for it out of other income. That might still be your choice. Make it on purpose, and write it down.

slides.title: Of the paid options, only the flat fee keeps Cedar Ridge's cash flow positive
slides.caption: All on the DSCR quote. Rows after Option B are assumptions. Before the $400/yr permit renewal found later; subtract $400 from each cash flow. Ranking unchanged.
slides.notes:
This table puts every option on the DSCR quote side by side.

Row three removes a duplicate. If the co-host covers inspections and after-hours response, the $150 retainer pays for the same work. Drop it, and cash flow improves by $1,800, to negative $5,998.

Row four changes the fee base. The same 18%, charged on nightly revenue only, is $11,448. Cash flow is negative $5,876. Each of those rows changes one thing from Option B. They don't stack.

Row five is a messaging-only co-host at 10%. Cash flow is negative $1,856. In the weak case it's negative $11,208.

The last row is a flat service at $400 a month. Cash flow stays positive at $772.

One adjustment. A later diligence step, PA.9, found a $400-a-year permit renewal. Take $400 off every cash flow here. The ranking doesn't change. We don't price a full manager, but any manager quote runs through this same test.

slides.title: Price owner time: a 10% co-host costs at least $81 for each hour it replaces
slides.side:
Hours from lesson 0.3: 1.5 per stay on messages, scheduling, and turnover checks. That's an upper bound. A messaging-only co-host replaces less.

Option B: $13,370 ÷ 91.5 = **about $146**. Flat $400/month service: $4,800 ÷ 91.5 = **about $52**.
slides.notes:
The cash flow math tells you what the house can carry. Your time needs a price too.

Use the time estimate for Maya and Chris from lesson 0.3: about 1.5 hours per stay on messages, scheduling, and turnover checks. That's an assumption. Across 61 stays, it's 91.5 hours a year. Their bookkeeping, pricing, and vendor calls are left out to keep it simple.

Treat 91.5 as the most a co-host could replace. A messaging-only co-host takes the messages, not the scheduling or turnover checks. So Option C's $7,428 works out to at least $81 per hour, and really more.

Option B, the 18% co-host, costs about $146 per hour. The flat $400 service costs about $52 per hour, with the same caveat.

So the question is whether an hour of their time is worth at least $81, when cash flow goes negative. There's no right answer on the slide. Put your own hours in and see what you're buying.

slides.title: Cedar Ridge picks a vendor set, with limits and a backup written into every row
slides.notes:
Given these numbers, Maya and Chris choose the vendor set and do the messaging themselves, with Chris as Maya's backup. The flat $400 service also stays positive, but only by $772, against $5,572 for the vendor set. They keep it as the first thing to try if messaging becomes too much.

Here's the team. The dollar limits are assumptions. The cleaner gets calendar access only. They make emergency supply top-ups up to $75 per turnover, with receipts. Maya orders routine supplies. The cleaner sees the guest's first name and party size, nothing more.

The handyman has no platform access. Maya sends tasks. He can spend up to $200 per job. His lock code works for job windows and emergency calls.

Maya's phone is on until 10 p.m. After that, calls forward to the handyman for urgent issues. Any fire, carbon monoxide, or injury goes to 911.

If they add a messaging co-host later, that person gets calendar and messaging access, not full access.
slides.keyline: The flat service stays positive but leaves only $772; they keep $5,572 by messaging themselves.
slides.caption: Guest data and key access for each role: see the lesson table. Dollar limits and response times are assumptions.

slides.title: Run your own cost check: find your break-even fee before you read any proposal
rows: Annual debt service (loan principal and interest)
Cash flow with vendor set = NOI - debt service
Break-even fee % = vendor-set cash flow ÷ gross
Proposed fee: % and base, then dollars
Cash flow with proposed setup = vendor-set cash flow - fee + duplicates removed
Weak case: gross, then cash flow with proposed setup
Owner hours replaced = hours per stay taken over × stays
Cost per owner hour = fee ÷ hours replaced
slides.caption: Part C of the exercise. Use your underwriting from Sam's PA.4, or your best estimate of a year's revenue and costs with a cleaner and handyman retainer included.
slides.notes:
The exercise has three parts. Part A is the task ledger. List every job from the job list. Beside each, write who does it, the backup, who pays, and how. If a task has two payers, fix it before you sign anything.

Part B is the access matrix. One row per person, including backups.

Part C is on the slide. It's the cost check. Use your own underwriting from Sam's PA.4. If you haven't done that, use your best estimate of a year's revenue and costs, with a cleaner and a handyman retainer in costs.

Work down the lines in order. Get your cash flow with a vendor set. Divide it by gross to get your break-even fee. Only then look at the proposal. Put in the fee, the base, and the dollars. Add back any duplicate costs it removes. Then run the same thing for the weak case, because the next slide needs it. Last, work out the cost per owner hour.

slides.title: Four decision rules settle the team before the calendar opens

gates.q: Is the proposed fee at or below your break-even fee?
gates.sub: Above it, the base case goes negative.
gates.no: Proceed only if you've decided to fund the gap from other income, in writing

gates.q: Can your reserves cover a year of the weak case with this setup?
gates.no: Reduce the scope or change the fee base

gates.q: Does every role have a trained backup?
Does anyone have more platform access than their row needs?

slides.end: All four pass: sign the agreements and hand the team to OP.8.
slides.notes:
These four rules turn the worksheet into a decision.

First, compare the proposed fee with your break-even fee. If it's higher, the base case goes negative. You can still go ahead. But only if you've decided to fund the gap from other income, and you've written that down. I want that decision on paper, not discovered in month four.

Second, check the weak case. If it goes negative by more than your reserves can cover for a year, reduce the scope or change the fee base. Before the permit renewal, the Cedar Ridge weak case is already -$5,475 with the vendor set, and -$11,208 with the 10% messaging co-host. Hold both against your reserve.

Third, every role needs a trained backup. If one doesn't have it, the calendar doesn't open.

Fourth, check access. If anyone has more platform access than their row requires, lower it now. It's easier on day one than after six months.

Pass all four, and the team is ready for its instructions.

slides.title: An attorney, the insurer, and the CPA each confirm a piece of the team setup
rows: Attorney or state real estate licensing board
Whether a paid co-host or manager needs a license in your state
Required vendor coverage, and whether a co-host or manager must be named on the policy
How co-host payouts through Airbnb are reported, and whether any contractor needs a year-end information return
Airbnb help pages and your account screens
Permission level names and what each allows, checked before you add anyone
slides.notes:
Four checks before this team goes live.

The attorney or the state real estate licensing board tells you whether a paid co-host or manager needs a license in your state. That's not something to guess at. It can affect the person you hire and the agreement you sign.

The insurer tells you what vendor coverage your policy requires. Ask whether a co-host or manager must be named or listed on the policy.

The CPA tells you how co-host payouts through Airbnb get reported. Remember, co-hosts are paid first, straight from the booking. Ask whether any contractor needs a year-end information return from you.

And check Airbnb's current co-host help pages against your own account screens. Airbnb changes these screens. Confirm what each level allows before you set up anyone's access.

slides.title: This week, name every role and backup and find your break-even fee
items: Write the task ledger: every job from the list, one doer, one payer.
Find your break-even fee: vendor-set cash flow ÷ gross booking revenue.
Fill in the access matrix at the lowest platform level each row needs.
Ask the state licensing board or your attorney if a paid co-host needs a license.
slides.next: Next: OP.8 SOPs writes the turnover checklist, message sequence, and emergency matrix for this team.
slides.notes:
Four actions this week.

Write your task ledger. Every job from the list, one person who does it, one person who pays for it. Watch for two names on one line.

Work out your break-even fee. Take your vendor-set cash flow from your underwriting and divide by gross booking revenue. Write it at the top of the page, so you see it when a quote comes in.

Fill in the access matrix. When you add each person on your platform, set their access to the lowest level their row needs. If someone already has more, lower it today.

And make one call about licensing, to the state board or your attorney.

You've named who does each job and what they can touch. Now they need instructions they can follow without calling you. That's OP.8. It writes the turnover checklist, the message sequence, and the emergency matrix for the Cedar Ridge team. Then it walks them through a normal turnover, a guest problem, and a real emergency.

slides.notes:
The platform rules in this lesson come from four Airbnb pages. I summarized them as of September 25, 2026. Airbnb changes these screens, so confirm the permission labels in your own account.

The co-host page, article 1534, covers the permission levels and the owner's responsibility for co-hosts. The resource center article gives background on the permission levels. The payouts page, article 3389, covers who sets up payouts and the rule that co-hosts are paid first. The Co-Host Additional Terms, article 3264, cover your responsibility for what a co-host did before you removed them.

The Cedar Ridge numbers come from the course's running example. That means the base case, the weak case, the 18% co-host case, and the two loan quotes. The new scenarios were computed for this lesson and marked as assumptions. That covers the 10% messaging co-host, the fee-base variant, the flat service, the break-even fee, and the owner hours.

Licensing rules aren't sourced here, because they depend on your state. Your attorney or the state licensing board confirms them.
